meta.title: Who really said "If you can't measure it, you can't manage it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Peter Drucker never wrote it, and no source has ever been found. W. Edwards Deming put the words in print only to call them a costly myth.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you can't measure it, you can't manage it'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Drucker, and not Deming either - he printed the line to call it a costly myth. An unsourced management maxim with no documented author.

answer.label: Not Peter Drucker — an unsourced management maxim
answer.authorDates: Unattributed · no documented author or first use
answer.sourceLine: Nothing resembling this sentence has been found in Peter Drucker’s published work; a Berkeley Haas faculty note ↗, citing the Drucker Institute’s own post, reports that Drucker did not originate the phrase. The words do appear in W. Edwards Deming’s The New Economics — but inside a sentence calling them “a costly myth” ↗.

source.heading: The paper trail

docMeta.dd: “If you can’t measure it, you can’t manage it”
The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education
W. Edwards Deming, who set the words down in order to reject them; the Deming Institute cites the third edition (MIT Press, 2018), p. 26

source.excerpt: It is wrong to suppose that if you can’t measure it, you can’t manage it – a costly myth.
trail: The W. Edwards Deming Institute files the line under “Myth” ↗, and explains that the short form is misattributed to Deming precisely because people quote a fragment of his sentence and reverse his meaning.
The Institute’s own quotations database gives the wording with a citation to The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education, third edition (MIT Press, 2018), p. 26 ↗.

A 2015 Berkeley Haas faculty note reports that neither Drucker nor Deming coined it ↗, citing each institute’s own post rather than any correspondence with them — and the Drucker Institute piece it links (“Measurement Myopia,” July 2013) is about the sibling slogan “what gets measured gets managed,” not this wording.

For the sibling slogan, the nearest candidate ancestor a 2012 hunt could find is not a management thinker at all: Lord Kelvin’s lecture of 3 May 1883, “Electrical Units of Measurement” ↗ — offered there as the most likely source of the idea, not of any of the popular wordings, and a claim about science rather than about managing people.
source.excerptNote: The appearance the Deming Institute documents is a refutation, not an endorsement. Strip the first six words and Deming appears to be saying the opposite of what he wrote.

source.rightsNote: The popular one-liner has no identifiable author and no traceable first publication, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. The sentence quoted above is a different matter: it is Deming’s, from The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education — first published in 1993 and still in print from MIT Press — so it remains in copyright and appears here as a short quotation for comment.

author.name: W. Edwards Deming
author.heading: The man who printed the words — to reject them
author.bio: Deming was the statistician whose teaching on variation and process control reshaped postwar Japanese manufacturing and, belatedly, American management. He is the person most often named as the source of “if you can’t measure it, you can’t manage it” — which is an irony, because the sentence is his only in the sense that he wrote it down to knock it over. His actual argument was that a good deal of what matters most in an organisation never appears in the figures, and that managing by the visible numbers alone is a disease rather than a discipline.

cite.sourceCitation: No source located in Peter Drucker’s published work. The wording is documented in print in W. Edwards Deming, The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education, 3rd ed. (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2018), 26 — where Deming calls it “a costly myth”; the book was first published in 1993.

misattribution.heading: A maxim in search of an author
misattribution.intro: This is a slogan with no parent, and the two biggest names in management have both been drafted for the job — one of them while arguing the opposite.

items.why: Drucker is the default author for any brisk-sounding management line, but no page reference has ever surfaced. A Berkeley Haas faculty note ↗ reports that Drucker did not originate this phrase, citing the Drucker Institute’s own post — which is itself about the sibling slogan “what gets measured gets managed.” His own position pointed the other way: in The Effective Executive he argued that knowledge work cannot be measured the way manual work can ↗.

Deming really did write these words — inside a sentence rejecting them. The Deming Institute files the line under “Myth” ↗ and notes that he treated attention to visible figures alone as one of management’s “deadly diseases,” and that plenty of unmeasurable things still have to be managed.

The same machinery runs on Drucker’s other measurement slogan. A 2012 hunt for its origin concluded the writer had never seen an actual reference that proves he said it ↗, and a later investigation reports the Drucker Institute saying the same while quoting Simon Caulkin’s summary of V. F. Ridgway’s 1956 paper on the dysfunctional consequences of performance measurement ↗.

The oldest respectable relative is Kelvin’s 1883 remark that knowledge you cannot put in numbers is “of a meagre and unsatisfactory kind” ↗ — a claim about the state of scientific knowledge, not a licence to stop managing whatever resists a number.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody has found an author. What the record does show is that the most-cited candidate put these exact words into print in order to call them “a costly myth” ↗.

context.heading: Why the wrong version won
lead: The line survives because it is convenient. It converts a hard question — is this worth doing? — into an easy one: can we put a number on it? And it arrives pre-loaded with authority, because somebody in the room always says Drucker said it.

What makes this more than a footnote is the direction of travel. Both of the men usually credited are on record resisting the idea: Drucker on the unmeasurability of knowledge work, Deming on the danger of managing only what shows up in the figures. The maxim that carries their names is the position they were arguing against.
context.detailsSummary: The dead link, the sibling slogan, and the 1956 paper underneath both
detailsBody: The Drucker Institute’s own treatment of the question — a July 2013 piece titled “Measurement Myopia” by Paul Zak — is no longer online at its former address. A 2020 post that catalogued the debunkings ↗ preserves its title, author and date.

Henry Mintzberg, who has no patience for the maxim either, opens his rebuttal by calling it “sheer nonsense” ↗ — and, tellingly, attributes it to nobody at all. The scholarly thread behind the sibling slogan runs instead to V. F. Ridgway’s 1956 paper in Administrative Science Quarterly, which granted that quantitative measures are useful but warned they are routinely over-trusted ↗.
context.pull: Deming did write these words. He wrote them so he could call them a costly myth.
